title: Advice, and Doing It Yourself
overview: This unit is about advice: giving it, asking for it, and deciding what to do with it. You will say what a person should or ought to do, and what they needn't do at all. You will say that you did a thing yourself, and name what you are responsible for, capable of and keen on. You will also count out of a group with either, neither, both of, several of and plenty of.
learningPath: Meet 28 words for advice, doing it alone, changing a habit and how you feel about it.
Read a conversation about studying, a page that argues for short study sessions, and a real notice.
Learn should and ought to for advice, and needn't for what is not necessary.
Learn myself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves and themselves.
Learn responsible for, capable of and keen on: the small word each one brings.
Learn the set phrases in writing, by hand, at last and on purpose.
Learn either, neither, both of, several of and plenty of, and the verb each one takes.
Speak, write, check every answer against the key, then take the quiz and record the assignment.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 19. This unit is about advice, and about doing things for yourself.
Advice is not an order. It is one person saying what they think is a good idea.
English has two words for that, and they mean the same thing.
Should. You should write it down.
Ought to. You ought to write it down.
Same advice. Pick either one.
There is one difference on the page. Ought keeps its to. Should never takes one.
You ought to go. You should go.
Now the other direction. Sometimes the useful thing to say is that a job is not necessary at all.
That word is needn't. You needn't ring them. The notice says it online.
You already know mustn't. Mustn't means it is forbidden. Needn't means there is no need.
You mustn't press this. You needn't press this. Two different sentences.
Next, doing it yourself.
Sometimes the person doing the action is the person it happens to.
I taught myself to cook. She reminded herself to take the form.
The word ends in self, and it matches the person in front of it.
I, myself. You, yourself. He, himself. She, herself. We, ourselves. They, themselves.
The same word does a second job. Put it after the noun and it means without help.
I filled the form in myself. They painted the room themselves.
That is the meaning of independent: able to do it and decide it without help.
Careful with one thing. English does not use these words after wash or dress.
I washed and got dressed. Not: I washed myself.
Next, three adjectives that bring a small word with them.
You already know good at, interested in and afraid of.
Here are three more. Responsible for. Capable of. Keen on.
I am responsible for the keys. She is capable of doing it alone. He is keen on early starts.
The small word never changes, so learn the pair and not the two words.
A verb after the small word takes ing. Capable of fixing it. Keen on studying at night.
Four more pairs come up in this unit.
Satisfied with. Disappointed with. Familiar with. Suitable for.
Next, set phrases.
Some phrases are fixed. The small word in front follows no rule you can work out.
In writing. By hand. At last. On purpose.
Please send it in writing. The form must be filled in by hand.
At last, the parcel arrived. He left the light on, on purpose.
Change the small word and the phrase stops meaning anything. Say the whole phrase, every time.
Last, counting out of a group.
Either means one of two, and it does not matter which. Either day is fine.
Neither means not one and not the other. Neither day is free.
Both of means the two together. Both of the forms are here.
Several of means more than two, but not many. Several of the answers were wrong.
Plenty of means more than enough. Plenty of time. Plenty of people.
Watch the verb. Either and neither take is, was and does.
Neither of my keys opens it. Both of, several of and plenty of take are, were and do.
Now the unit itself.
You will read a conversation between you and a classmate about studying in the evening.
Then a page that argues one thing: do less, and do it more often.
Then a real notice from a self study room, with rules you can actually follow.
The advice in this unit is about learning English and about ordinary tasks. Nothing more.
Every practice has an answer key under it. Do the practice, then check, then count.
For the speaking tasks, record yourself and play it back. Your own ear is the check.
One last tip, and it is the tip the second reading argues for.
Twenty minutes on six days beats two hours on one day. A habit costs no effort once it is built.
Start the unit now. Take the words first, then the five cards in order.

outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 1 practice, seven of eight; Practice 2, six of eight; Speaking 1 recording played back with the plain verb after every modal.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can tell someone what they should do and what they needn't do.

outcomes.outcome: Use myself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves and themselves when the person doing the action is also the person it happens to.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 2 practice, seven of eight; Practice 3, six of eight; Speaking 2 recording with one self word to a sentence.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say that I did something myself.

outcomes.outcome: Say and write what you are responsible for, capable of and keen on, keeping the small word each adjective brings with it.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 3 practice, seven of eight; Practice 1 and Practice 4; Writing 2 checked against its criteria.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write what I am responsible for and what I am keen on.

outcomes.outcome: Use the set phrases in writing, by hand, at last and on purpose without changing the small word in front of them.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 4 practice, six of eight; Practice 4; Writing 3, which must carry four of the phrases.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can use set phrases like in writing and by hand with the right small word.

outcomes.outcome: Choose between either, neither, both of, several of and plenty of, and match the verb to the one you chose.
outcomes.evidence: Grammar card 5 practice, six of eight; Practice 5, six of eight; quiz items 11 and 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can choose between either, neither, both of and plenty of, and use the right verb.

outcomes.outcome: Follow spoken advice closely enough to separate the advice itself from the reason given for it.

words.meaning: What another person tells you they think you should do.
words.example: Can I ask you for some advice?
practice: Her advice was short and useful.
I took the advice and it worked.
That is good advice, but it is hard to follow.
Nobody asked for my advice.
words.starter: The best advice I ever got was …
words.tutor: Give me three short problems about studying, one at a time, and let me answer each with one piece of advice.

words.meaning: To tell someone what you think they should do.
words.example: The person at the desk advised me to come back on Monday.
practice: I advise you to read the notice first.
She advised him to keep a list.
What would you advise?
They advised me against the long evenings.
words.starter: I would advise you to …
words.tutor: Ask me what I would advise in four everyday situations, and tell me if I used advise with a person after it.

words.meaning: Help of a general kind, given over time, to show you the way.
words.example: New workers get guidance for the first month.
practice: The notice gives clear guidance on booking a desk.
I looked for guidance and found none.
Her guidance made the first week easier.
The card on the wall is there for guidance.
words.starter: I would like some guidance on …
words.tutor: Explain the difference between a tip, advice and guidance, then test me with six examples.

words.meaning: To say things that make someone want to keep going.
words.example: She encouraged me to try again.
practice: A short win encourages you to come back tomorrow.
He encouraged us to speak, even with mistakes.
Nobody encouraged her, and she carried on anyway.
I encourage myself by counting the days I studied.
words.starter: What encourages me most is …
words.tutor: Give me four things a person might say to encourage somebody, and I will say which one I would find useful.

words.meaning: To say or do things that make someone want to stop.
words.example: The long list discouraged me at first.
practice: Do not let one bad week discourage you.
A hard test can discourage a new learner.
He tried to discourage me from starting at all.
Silence discourages people more than a correction does.
words.starter: The thing that discourages me is …
words.tutor: Say four sentences and I will tell you whether each one encourages or discourages, and why.

words.meaning: To tell someone that something may be dangerous or may go wrong.
words.example: The notice warns you that the floor is wet.
practice: I warned him that the shop shuts at four.
She warns every new person about the slow computer.
Nobody warned me about the queue.
The card on the wall warns you not to repair anything.
words.starter: I want to warn you about …
words.tutor: Give me four notices you might see in a building, and I will say what each one warns you about.

words.meaning: To say calm, true things to someone who is worried.
words.example: He reassured me that the form was right.
practice: A short answer reassures people more than a long one.
She reassured the group that there was plenty of time.
I reassured myself by reading the notice again.
Nothing he said reassured me.
words.starter: It reassures me when somebody says …
words.tutor: I will say a worry. Reassure me in one sentence, then ask me to do the same for you.

words.meaning: One short, useful piece of help.
words.example: Here is a tip: say the word out loud.
practice: That tip saved me twenty minutes.
She gave me two tips for the test.
The best tip in this unit is the shortest one.
I keep a list of tips at the back of my notebook.
words.starter: My best tip for learning words is …
words.tutor: Give me five tips for studying English at night, and I will pick the two I could start today.

words.meaning: The word for me, when I am the person the action happens to, or when nobody helped me.
words.example: I taught myself to cook.
practice: I filled the form in myself.
I cut myself on the tin.
I asked myself why I stopped.
I was working by myself all evening.
words.starter: I did it myself when I …
words.tutor: Ask me four questions that I must answer with myself in the sentence.

words.meaning: The word for you, when you are the person the action happens to, or when nobody helped you.
words.example: Did you fill the form in yourself?
practice: Help yourself to a mug.
You should give yourself twenty minutes, no more.
Did you build that yourself?
Do not push yourself on a tired evening.
words.starter: You can do this yourself if you …
words.tutor: Give me four pieces of advice that each use yourself, and tell me if I ever write your self as two words.

words.meaning: The word for him, when he is the person the action happens to, or when nobody helped him.
words.example: He taught himself to drive.
practice: He wrote the note himself.
He was sitting by himself at the back.
He reminded himself to take the receipt.
He fixed the chair himself and it still wobbles.
words.starter: He did it himself, so …
words.tutor: Tell me a short story about a man doing things alone, and stop four times for me to add himself.

words.meaning: The word for her, when she is the person the action happens to, or when nobody helped her.
words.example: She reminded herself to take the form.
practice: She booked the desk herself.
She is capable of doing it herself.
She let herself into the room.
She was studying by herself until eight.
words.starter: She did it herself because …
words.tutor: Ask me four questions about a woman working alone, and check that I use herself and not her self.

words.meaning: The word for us, when we are the people the action happens to, or when nobody helped us.
words.example: We painted the room ourselves.
practice: We gave ourselves one hour and no more.
We booked both of the desks ourselves.
We found the answer ourselves in the end.
We were sitting by ourselves in the quiet corner.
words.starter: We did it ourselves, and …
words.tutor: Give me four sentences about two people working without help, each using ourselves.

words.meaning: The word for them, when they are the people the action happens to, or when nobody helped them.
words.example: They repaired the door themselves.
practice: They taught themselves from a book.
They should give themselves more time.
Several of them study by themselves at night.
They asked themselves the same question.
words.starter: They did it themselves after …
words.tutor: Say four sentences about a group doing a job alone, and tell me if I use themself, which is not a word here.

words.meaning: Able to do things and decide things without help.
words.example: Short daily study makes you more independent.
practice: She is very independent and rarely asks for help.
This unit is for independent study.
Being independent does not mean refusing advice.
He became independent after the first month.
words.starter: I am independent when it comes to …
words.tutor: Ask me four questions about what I can already do without help, and use the word independent in each one.

words.meaning: Always doing what it said it would do, so people can depend on it.
words.example: The old bus is slow but reliable.
practice: She is the most reliable person on the team.
I need a reliable way to remember new words.
The lift is not reliable, so use the stairs.
A short habit is more reliable than a long plan.
words.starter: The most reliable thing in my week is …
words.tutor: Give me four things and I will say whether each is reliable, and what would make it more reliable.

words.meaning: Something you do so often that you do it without deciding.
words.example: Studying at the same time every day becomes a habit.
practice: A habit is built out of small days.
It took a month to develop the habit.
I have the habit of reading on the bus.
Breaking a habit is harder than starting one.
words.starter: One habit I would like to develop is …
words.tutor: Ask me about one habit I want to start, then help me pick a time that already exists in my day.

words.meaning: The work you put in when a thing is not easy.
words.example: A habit costs no effort once it is built.
practice: Twenty minutes takes very little effort.
She made a real effort with the writing task.
The effort is worth it in the end.
It takes effort to speak out loud when you are tired.
words.starter: The task that takes me the most effort is …
words.tutor: Ask me which part of learning English takes me the most effort, and suggest one way to make it smaller.

words.meaning: To grow or build something slowly, step by step.
words.example: You develop a habit by repeating it, not by planning it.
practice: I am developing a way to remember new words.
Her English developed quickly in the second year.
The town developed around the market.
It takes weeks to develop a reliable routine.
words.starter: I want to develop …
words.tutor: Help me develop one small study routine, and ask me what would stop me on a tired day.

words.meaning: To reach something you worked for.
words.example: You achieve more in twenty minutes than in a tired hour.
practice: She achieved a good result without help.
What do you want to achieve this month?
I achieved nothing on Tuesday and a lot on Wednesday.
Count what you achieved, not what you planned.
words.starter: This month I want to achieve …
words.tutor: Ask me what I want to achieve this month, then help me cut it into four smaller parts.

words.meaning: To find something very hard and to keep trying anyway.
words.example: Everybody struggles with some weeks.
practice: I struggle with long readings.
He struggled to fill the form in by hand.
They struggled at first and then it became easy.
If you struggle with a word, say it out loud five times.
words.starter: I struggle most with …
words.tutor: Ask me what I struggle with in English, and give me one smaller first step for it.

words.meaning: To manage something difficult well enough to carry on.
words.example: Some weeks you cope and no more, and that is enough.
practice: She copes well with a long shift.
I cannot cope with two hours of study in one go.
How do you cope when you are tired?
Short sessions help me cope with a busy week.
words.starter: I cope with a busy week by …
words.tutor: Ask me how I cope on a busy day, and suggest the smallest useful thing I could still do.

words.meaning: Having enough skill to do a thing.
words.example: She is capable of doing it alone.
practice: You are capable of more than one page a day.
He is a capable driver.
I am not capable of that yet, but I will be.
The old machine is still capable of the job.
words.starter: I am capable of …
words.tutor: Ask me four questions using capable of, and check that I put ing on the verb after of.

words.meaning: Right for the job or for the person.
words.example: This room is suitable for quiet study.
practice: That desk is not suitable for two people.
Is this form suitable for a weekly booking?
Find a suitable time and keep it.
The shoes were not suitable for the walk.
words.starter: A suitable time for me to study is …
words.tutor: Give me four times of day and I will say which are suitable for study and why.

words.meaning: Known to you already, because you have met it before.
words.example: The word looked familiar but I could not use it.
practice: I am familiar with this form now.
Her face was familiar.
Start with familiar words, then add one new one.
The route is familiar, so I stop thinking about it.
words.starter: I am familiar with …
words.tutor: Give me six words from this unit and I will say which are familiar and which are new.

words.meaning: Happy enough with what you got.
words.example: I was satisfied with six out of eight.
practice: She is satisfied with the answer.
Are you satisfied with this month?
He was not satisfied and asked again.
I am satisfied with slow, steady progress.
words.starter: I am satisfied with …
words.tutor: Ask me what I am satisfied with this month, and make sure I use with after satisfied.

words.meaning: Sad because a thing was not as good as you hoped.
words.example: They were disappointed with the result.
practice: I was disappointed with my score, so I did it again.
Do not be disappointed after one bad week.
She sounded disappointed on the phone.
He was disappointed with himself and said so.
words.starter: I was disappointed with …
words.tutor: Ask me about a time I was disappointed, and help me turn it into one piece of advice.

words.meaning: Being the person who has to look after something, or who caused it.
words.example: You are responsible for your own things in this room.
practice: Who is responsible for the keys?
I am responsible for choosing the sentence.
He is responsible for locking up at night.
Nobody is responsible for your habit but you.
words.starter: I am responsible for …
words.tutor: Ask me four questions with responsible for, and tell me if I ever write responsible of.

grammar.title: Should, ought to, and needn't
grammar.explanation: Advice is not an order. Should and ought to say that a thing is a good idea, not that it is necessary. They mean the same, and should is the commoner of the two. Needn't goes the other way: it says the job is not necessary at all. After all three, the verb keeps its plain form.
grammar.rule:
You should write it down.
You ought to write it down.
Same advice. Ought keeps its to; should never takes one.
Not: You should to write it down.
Not: You ought write it down.
Advice against something:
You shouldn't leave it until Friday.
Question:
Should I ring them first?
Not necessary:
You needn't ring them. The notice says it online.
You already know mustn't. Compare the two:
You mustn't press this. (it is forbidden)
You needn't press this. (there is no need)
The verb after all of them is plain: go, ring, write, wait.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: it is a good idea to book the desk, and there is no need to ring.
Two pieces of advice, so two sentences.
The first is a good idea, so use should or ought to.
Pick should. The verb stays plain: book.
You should book the desk.
The second says there is no need, so use needn't.
The verb stays plain again: ring.
You needn't ring.
Now join the reason on: You should book the desk, but you needn't ring.
Check one thing: no to after should, and no to after needn't.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write You should to wait, because so many verbs take to in front of them. Should takes none: You should wait. Ought is the one that keeps it: You ought to wait. The other slip is using mustn't where you mean needn't. You mustn't book a desk says booking is forbidden. You needn't book a desk says you may, and there is no need.
grammar.tip: Should and ought to give the same advice; only ought to keeps its to.
grammar.practice:
Write each sentence again with the word in brackets. Keep the verb plain.
1. It is a good idea to write it down. (should)
2. It is a good idea to write it down. (ought to)
3. There is no need to fill in the long form. (needn't)
4. It is a bad idea to leave it until Friday. (shouldn't)
5. Is it a good idea for me to ring them first? (should)
6. There is no need for you to copy the page out. (needn't)
7. It is a good idea for her to give herself twenty minutes. (ought to)
8. It is a bad idea to study for three hours when you are tired. (shouldn't)
grammar.answers:
1. You should write it down.
2. You ought to write it down.
3. You needn't fill in the long form.
4. You shouldn't leave it until Friday.
5. Should I ring them first?
6. You needn't copy the page out.
7. She ought to give herself twenty minutes.
8. You shouldn't study for three hours when you are tired.
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing You should to write it down. Should takes no to.
Item 3 catches people the other way, as You mustn't fill in the long form. That would forbid it.
Seven or eight right: go on. Five or six: read the rule again and do 1 to 4 once more.

grammar.title: Myself, yourself, herself: the same person twice
grammar.explanation: Sometimes the person doing the action is the person it happens to. English marks that with a word ending in self. I cut myself. She taught herself. The self word matches the person in front of it. It does a second job too: put it after the noun and it means without help.
grammar.rule:
I: myself
you, one person: yourself
he: himself
she: herself
we: ourselves
they: themselves
The doer is also the one it happens to:
I taught myself to cook.
She reminded herself to take the form.
After the noun it means without help:
I filled the form in myself.
They painted the room themselves.
With by it means alone:
He was working by himself.
Careful: English does not use these after wash or dress.
I washed and got dressed. Not: I washed myself.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: she booked the desk, and nobody helped her.
Start with the plain sentence: She booked the desk.
Now add the without help part. That needs a self word.
Ask who did it. She did, so the self word is herself.
Put it at the end: She booked the desk herself.
Now a different meaning. She is the one the action happens to.
She reminded who? She reminded her own self.
So the self word goes straight after the verb: She reminded herself.
Answer: She booked the desk herself, and she reminded herself to take the form.
Check one thing: the self word matches she, so it is herself and not himself.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write She reminded her to take the form when you mean her own self. That sentence is about a second woman. If the doer and the person it happens to are the same, the word must end in self: She reminded herself. The other slip is writing your self or them self as two words. They are one word each: yourself, themselves.
grammar.tip: Same person twice, so the word ends in self. One self word to a sentence.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing self word in each sentence.
1. I taught ____ to cook.
2. She reminded ____ to take the receipt.
3. He was sitting by ____ at the back.
4. We gave ____ one hour and no more.
5. They repaired the door ____ .
6. Did you fill the form in ____ ?
7. Help ____ to a mug of tea.
8. She is capable of doing it ____ .
grammar.answers:
1. myself  2. herself  3. himself  4. ourselves  5. themselves  6. yourself  7. yourself  8. herself
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: writing her. She reminded her is about a second woman.
Item 5 catches people as themself, which is not used here. They takes themselves.
Seven or eight right: go on. Five or six: cover the answers and do the list again.

grammar.title: Responsible for, capable of, keen on
grammar.explanation: Some adjectives cannot finish an idea alone. They bring a small word with them, and that small word never changes. Responsible takes for. Capable takes of. Keen takes on. You already know good at, interested in and afraid of. After the small word comes a noun or an ing verb.
grammar.rule:
responsible for: I am responsible for the keys.
capable of: She is capable of doing it alone.
keen on: He is keen on early starts.
A verb after the small word takes ing:
capable of fixing it
keen on studying at night
responsible for locking up
Four more pairs in this unit:
satisfied with the answer
disappointed with the result
familiar with the form
suitable for the job
The small word is part of the adjective. Learn the pair, not the two words.
Not: responsible of. Not: capable to. Not: keen of.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: you can fix the chair, and looking after the keys is your job.
Take the first half. Can do it means capable.
Capable brings of with it: capable of.
After of a verb takes ing: fixing.
I am capable of fixing the chair.
Take the second half. It is your job means responsible.
Responsible brings for with it: responsible for.
A noun follows, so no ing is needed: the keys.
I am responsible for the keys.
Answer: I am capable of fixing the chair, and I am responsible for the keys.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write I am responsible of the keys, because of feels like the everyday joiner. Responsible takes for: responsible for the keys. The second common slip is capable to do it. Capable takes of, and the verb after of ends in ing: capable of doing it.
grammar.tip: Learn the pair as one item: responsible for, capable of, keen on.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing small word. Use for, of, on or with.
1. I am responsible ____ the keys.
2. She is capable ____ doing it alone.
3. He is keen ____ early starts.
4. Are you satisfied ____ the answer?
5. They were disappointed ____ the result.
6. I am familiar ____ this form now.
7. This room is suitable ____ quiet study.
8. Nobody is responsible ____ your habit but you.
grammar.answers:
1. for  2. of  3. on  4. with  5. with  6. with  7. for  8. for
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing of. Responsible always takes for.
Item 3 catches people as keen of. Keen takes on, like good at and interested in.
Seven or eight right: go on. Five or six: write the eight pairs out and read them aloud twice.

grammar.title: In writing, by hand, at last, on purpose
grammar.explanation: Some phrases are fixed. The small word in front follows no rule you can work out, so you learn the whole phrase as one item. In writing. By hand. At last. On purpose. Change the small word and the phrase stops meaning anything at all.
grammar.rule:
in writing: Please send it in writing.
by hand: The form must be filled in by hand.
at last: At last, the parcel arrived.
on purpose: He left the light on, on purpose.
More you will meet in this unit:
at first: At first it was hard.
in the end: In the end I gave up.
on time: The bus came on time.
by mistake: I took the wrong bag by mistake.
in person: Come in person, not by phone.
Say the whole phrase, never the two words apart.
Not: on writing. Not: with hand. Not: at purpose.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: after a long wait the letter came, and the office wants a written note.
Take the long wait first. The fixed phrase for that is at last.
Do not try to build it. At last is learnt whole.
At last, the letter came.
Now the written note. The fixed phrase is in writing.
Not on writing, not by writing. In writing.
The office wants it in writing.
Answer: At last, the letter came, and the office wants my reply in writing.
Check one thing: each phrase is spelt exactly as you learnt it, small word included.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write with hand instead of by hand, because with is the word for the thing you use. This phrase is fixed and takes by: filled in by hand. The other slip is at the end for at last. At the end names a place in time; at last means after a long wait.
grammar.tip: These phrases have no rule inside them. Learn each one whole, small word first.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing small word. Use in, by, at or on.
1. Please send your answer ____ writing.
2. The form must be filled in ____ hand.
3. ____ last, the parcel arrived.
4. He left the light on, ____ purpose.
5. ____ first it was hard, and then it was easy.
6. I took the wrong bag ____ mistake.
7. The bus came ____ time for once.
8. Come ____ person, not by phone.
grammar.answers:
1. in  2. by  3. At  4. on  5. At  6. by  7. on  8. in
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: writing with hand. The fixed phrase is by hand.
Item 3 catches people as In last. There is no such phrase; it is at last.
Six or more right: go on. Five or fewer: copy the eight phrases out and use four in sentences of your own.

grammar.title: Either, neither, both of, plenty of
grammar.explanation: These words say how many out of a group. Either means one of two and it does not matter which. Neither means not one and not the other. Both of means the two together. Several of means more than two but not many. Plenty of means more than enough. Watch the verb after each one.
grammar.rule:
Two only:
Either day is fine.
Neither day is free.
Either of the two forms is fine.
Neither of my keys opens it.
The two together:
Both of the forms are here.
Both forms are here. (of goes when the goes)
More than two:
Several of the answers were wrong.
Plenty of people use this room.
The verb:
Either and neither take is, was, does, opens.
Both of, several of and plenty of take are, were, do, open.
Not: Neither of my keys open it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: you have two keys, you tried them, and the door stayed shut.
Two things only, and not one of them worked.
Not one and not the other is neither.
Neither of my keys.
Now the verb. Neither counts as one, so the verb is the he and she form.
Opens, not open.
Neither of my keys opens the door.
Change it to the two together and both takes are: Both of my keys are old.
Check one thing: neither and either take the short verb, both of does not.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write Neither of my keys open it, because keys is plural and sits right in front of the verb. Neither counts as one thing: Neither of my keys opens it. The other slip is dropping the: both of forms. Of needs the after it, or leave of out and write both forms.
grammar.tip: Either and neither are one; both of, several of and plenty of are more than one.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right word or verb form.
1. (Either / Both) day is fine. I do not mind which.
2. (Neither / Several) of my keys opens that door. I tried them both.
3. (Both of / Either of) the forms are here on the desk.
4. (Several / Plenty) of the answers were wrong, so I did it again.
5. There is (several / plenty) of time before the room shuts.
6. Neither of the days (is / are) free this week.
7. Both of the quiet corners (was / were) taken by six.
8. Plenty of people (uses / use) this room after work.
grammar.answers:
1. Either  2. Neither  3. Both of  4. Several  5. plenty  6. is  7. were  8. use
The likeliest wrong answer is 6: writing are, because days is plural. Neither counts as one.
Item 5 catches people as several. Several counts things; there is several of time is not English.
Six or more right: go on. Five or fewer: read the verb lines on the card again and redo 6 to 8.

readings.title: Ask me for advice
readings.setting: A study room at an English school, at the end of the day
readings.passage:
You: Can I ask you something? I am not satisfied with my English this month.
Nadia: Of course. What is the trouble?
You: I study every evening, but I forget everything by the weekend.
Nadia: How long do you sit down for?
You: Two hours. Sometimes three.
Nadia: That is the problem, I think. You ought to study for twenty minutes, but every day.
You: Twenty minutes is nothing.
Nadia: It is nothing on Monday. It is a lot by the end of the month. A habit is built out of small days.
You: So I should cut the long evenings?
Nadia: You should cut them, yes. And you needn't write every new word down. You needn't copy the page out by hand either.
You: Then what do I write?
Nadia: Write the sentence you would actually say. One sentence for each word. You are responsible for choosing it, so you remember it.
You: I am not capable of that yet.
Nadia: You are. You did the last test yourself and you passed it.
You: That was luck.
Nadia: It was not luck. Listen: neither of us learns this in a month. Both of us are slow. Plenty of people give up in week three, and you have not.
You: That is kind.
Nadia: It is not kindness, it is the truth. One more tip. Say it out loud. Reading in silence feels like work and teaches you less.
You: At last, some advice I can start tonight.
Nadia: Start tonight, then. And do not tell me tomorrow that you were too tired.
You: I will not. I will do it myself and count the days.
Nadia: Count the days, not the hours. That is the whole thing.

readings.title: Small, and every day
readings.setting: A page from a short guide for adult learners
readings.passage:
Most advice about learning a language is about time. Find more time, people say. Get up earlier. Give up your evening.
In my view that advice is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that makes people stop.
Here is the argument. A long evening of study feels serious, so we trust it. But a long evening is hard to repeat. You do it on Monday, you are too tired on Tuesday, and by Thursday the plan has gone. A short session is easy to repeat, and repeating is the part that works.
So the advice ought to be the other way round. Do less, and do it more often. Twenty minutes on six days beats two hours on one.
There is a second reason, and it is not about time at all. When you study for a long time, you are mostly reading. When you study for a short time, you choose the one thing you actually need, and you say it out loud. Choosing is the work. It is also the part nobody can do for you.
That is why the habit matters more than the hour. A habit costs no effort once it is built, and the effort of building it is smaller than people think. Pick a time that already exists in your day: the bus, the queue, the ten minutes before the shop opens.
None of this is a promise. You will still struggle with some weeks, and some weeks you will cope and no more. But if you are keen on results you can see, count the days you studied and not the hours.
Plenty of people never count anything. Then they are disappointed with a month they cannot remember.

readings.title: Self-study room: how it works
readings.setting: A board by the door of a self-study room
readings.passage:
SELF-STUDY ROOM
Open every weekday, from 8 in the morning until 8 at night.
Booking a desk
Desks 1 to 12 may be booked. Ask at the desk by the door and write your name in the book by hand.
We do not take bookings by phone. Come in person.
If you want a desk for a whole week, put it in writing and give the note to the person at the desk.
Desks 13 to 20 are not booked. Sit at either of them if it is free.
While you are here
You are responsible for your own things. The room is not locked at lunch.
Return the headphones to the box before you leave.
You needn't book to read here. Come in and sit down.
Turn your phone to silent. If you need to talk, use the small room opposite.
If something is wrong
Report a broken chair, a broken socket or a slow computer in writing.
There is a card on the wall for this. Write what is wrong and the number of the desk.
Do not try to repair anything yourself.
Plenty of people use this room after work, so it is busiest between 5 and 7.
Both of the quiet corners are usually taken by 6.
Anything left behind is kept for one month. Ask at the desk.

comprehension.q: What does Nadia say you ought to do instead of studying for two or three hours?
comprehension.a: Study for twenty minutes, but every day.
comprehension.why: She says it in one line: you ought to study for twenty minutes, but every day. The word every carries the point.

comprehension.q: Nadia says a habit is built out of small days. What does habit mean here?
comprehension.a: Something you do so often that you stop deciding to do it.
comprehension.why: Built out of small days tells you it grows by repeating. That is a habit, not one big effort.

comprehension.q: Why does Nadia say the last test was not luck?
comprehension.a: Because you did it yourself and passed, which shows you are capable.
comprehension.why: She answers I am not capable of that yet with the test. The test is her evidence, so luck is not her reading of it.

comprehension.q: What is the writer's main reason for saying a short session works better than a long one?
comprehension.a: A short session is easy to repeat, and repeating is the part that works.
comprehension.why: The third paragraph gives the whole argument: a long evening is hard to repeat, a short one is easy, and repeating is what does the work.

comprehension.q: Does the writer think find more time is good advice, and how do you know?
comprehension.a: No. The writer says in my view that advice is wrong.
comprehension.why: In my view marks an opinion, and the words after it say wrong. The rest of the page is the reason for that opinion.

comprehension.q: The writer says you will still struggle with some weeks. What does struggle mean here?
comprehension.a: Find it very hard, and keep going anyway.
comprehension.why: The next line says some weeks you will cope and no more, so the writer expects you to carry on. Struggle here is difficulty, not stopping.

comprehension.q: You want desk 5 for tomorrow only. What exactly does the notice tell you to do?
comprehension.a: Ask at the desk by the door and write your name in the book by hand.
comprehension.why: Desk 5 is in the range 1 to 12, so it is bookable, and the notice names the two steps for a single day.

comprehension.type: What a person would do next
comprehension.q: Your chair is broken. What does the notice tell you to do, and what does it tell you not to do?
comprehension.a: Report it in writing on the card on the wall, with what is wrong and the desk number, and do not repair it yourself.
comprehension.why: The If something is wrong part names the card, the two details to write, and the one thing the notice forbids.

comprehension.q: You arrive at half past six and want a quiet corner. What does the notice suggest will happen?
comprehension.a: Both quiet corners will probably already be taken.
comprehension.why: The notice says both of the quiet corners are usually taken by 6, and half past six is after that. Usually makes it likely, not certain.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Should, ought to, needn't
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud. Then record them and play them back.
You should write it down.
You ought to write it down.
You shouldn't leave it until Friday.
Should I ring them first?
You needn't fill in the long form.
You needn't book a desk to read here.
She ought to give herself twenty minutes.
You mustn't press this, but you needn't press that one either.
Now make eight of your own about a habit you want to start. You may invent every detail.
Play the recording back.
Check one thing only: listen for a to after should. There should be none.
Then check the verb after each modal. It stays plain: go, ring, write, wait.
speaking.tutor: Give me six situations from an ordinary day, one at a time, and I will answer each with one should sentence and one needn't sentence.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — I did it myself
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud, then record them and play them back.
I taught myself to cook.
I filled the form in myself.
She reminded herself to take the receipt.
He was sitting by himself at the back.
We gave ourselves one hour and no more.
They repaired the door themselves.
Did you fill the form in yourself?
She is capable of doing it herself.
Now say eight of your own about things you have done without help. You may invent them.
Play the recording back and count the self words.
One to a sentence is right. Check that each one matches the person: I with myself, she with herself.
speaking.tutor: Say four short sentences about a person working alone and stop before the last word each time, so I can finish it with the right self word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Responsible for, capable of, keen on
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud, then record them and play them back.
I am responsible for the keys.
I am responsible for locking up.
She is capable of doing it alone.
He is capable of fixing it himself.
I am keen on early starts.
I am keen on studying at night.
I am familiar with this form now, and satisfied with the answer.
They were disappointed with the result, but the room is suitable for quiet study.
Now say eight of your own. Use each of the three pairs twice. You may invent every detail.
Play the recording back and listen for the small word after each adjective.
Responsible for. Capable of. Keen on. If one is missing or wrong, say that line again.
speaking.tutor: Ask me eight questions that each need responsible for, capable of or keen on in the answer, and tell me every time I use the wrong small word.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Advice I would take, advice I would not
speaking.instructions:
Here are five pieces of advice from this unit.
Study for twenty minutes every day, not two hours once a week.
Say every new word out loud.
Write one sentence for each new word, not the meaning.
Count the days you studied, not the hours.
Pick a time that already exists in your day.
Record yourself answering each one in two sentences.
First sentence: what you think of it. I think that is good advice. I am not keen on that one.
Second sentence: your reason. It starts with because, so or but.
Play the recording back and count five pairs of sentences.
Check that every second sentence gives a reason and not a second opinion.
If someone is with you, say the same five turns to them and let them ask why. Doing it alone is fine.
speaking.tutor: Give me one piece of study advice at a time. I will say what I think and why, and you tell me if my reason really is a reason.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — The advice and the reason
speaking.instructions:
Play Reading 1 again and listen. Do not read it yet.
Nadia gives four pieces of advice. Each one comes with a reason or with nothing.
Listen once and write the four pieces of advice in short words.
Listen again and write the reason beside each one, or a dash where she gives none.
Then read the text and check.
The key: study twenty minutes every day, because a habit is built out of small days.
Do not write every word down, no reason given.
Write the sentence you would say, because you chose it, so you remember it.
Say it out loud, because reading in silence teaches you less.
Now record yourself saying each piece of advice with its reason joined by because.
Four out of four: go on. Two or three: play it once more and write only the reasons.
speaking.tutor: Read me a short piece of advice with a reason in it, then ask me to say back the advice and the reason separately.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — One minute of advice
speaking.instructions:
Record one minute of advice for someone starting this course next month.
Say three things they should or ought to do.
Say one thing they needn't do at all.
Say one thing you did yourself, using a self word.
Say what they will be responsible for and what they are already capable of.
End with what you think is the single best tip, and why.
Play it back once and count the six things in that list.
If one is missing, record the whole minute again. Do not add it in your head.
Check one more thing: no to after should, and the verb plain after needn't.
speaking.tutor: Listen to my one minute of advice as a plan, then ask me three questions a new learner would really ask.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Three things they should do, one they needn't
writing.prompt: Write four sentences of advice for someone who is starting to learn English this month. Three sentences say what they should or ought to do. One sentence says what they needn't do. You may invent every detail.
writing.model:
You should study for twenty minutes every day, not for two hours on Sunday.
You ought to say every new word out loud, even when you are alone.
You should write one sentence for each word, and choose the sentence yourself.
You needn't copy the whole page out by hand.
writing.starter: You should study for twenty minutes
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Three use should or ought to. One uses needn't. No to after should or after needn't. The verb after each one is plain. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
writing.support: Do one first, in two steps. Write the advice as a plain order: Study for twenty minutes every day. Then put You should in front and take nothing else away.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence that gives the reason for one piece of advice, joined with because.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Responsible for, capable of, keen on
writing.prompt: Write five sentences about yourself. Say one thing you are responsible for and one thing you are capable of. Then say one thing you are keen on, one you are satisfied with and one you were disappointed with. You may invent every detail, at work or where you study.
writing.model:
I am responsible for locking up the room at the end of the day.
I am capable of reading a short notice without a dictionary.
I am keen on studying early, before anybody else is awake.
I am satisfied with six days out of seven this month.
I was disappointed with my score in the last test, so I did it again.
writing.criteria: Five sentences. Each one uses a different adjective from the list. The small word after each adjective is right: for, of, on, with, with. Any verb after the small word ends in ing.
writing.support: Write the five adjectives in a column first: responsible, capable, keen, satisfied, disappointed. Write the small word beside each one. Then build the sentence around the pair.
writing.extension: Add a sixth sentence using familiar with or suitable for.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A short note with the set phrases
writing.prompt: Write a short note of six sentences to the person who looks after a study room. Ask for a desk for a week and report a broken chair. Use four of these phrases: in writing, by hand, at last, on purpose, on time, in person. You may invent every detail.
writing.model:
I am writing to ask for desk 7 for the whole of next week.
The notice says a weekly booking must be put in writing, so here it is.
I filled the card in by hand because the computer at the door was slow.
I am also reporting the chair at desk 12. One leg is loose.
Nobody broke it on purpose, but it is not safe to sit on.
At last the room is quiet in the mornings, and I would like to keep that desk.
writing.starter: I am writing to ask for
writing.criteria: Six sentences. Four of the set phrases appear, each spelt with its own small word. The note asks for the desk and reports the chair. Every sentence has a capital letter and a full stop.
writing.support: Write the four phrases you will use in a line first. Then write one sentence for each, and add two more sentences to join them up.
writing.extension: Add one more sentence using either in the end or by mistake.

writing.title: Writing 4 — What I think of that advice
writing.prompt: Reading 2 says: do less, and do it more often. Write two short paragraphs saying what you think of that advice. You may invent every detail.
writing.model:
I think that advice is right, and I am satisfied with what it did for me.
I used to study for three hours on one evening and nothing for the rest of the week.
Now I give myself twenty minutes a day, and I am familiar with more words than before.
But I am not keen on every part of it.
Some tasks are too long for twenty minutes, so I still need one longer evening a week.
In my view the best tip is the last one: count the days, not the hours.
writing.criteria: Two paragraphs, three sentences each. Paragraph one says what you agree with and gives a reason. Paragraph two says what you do not agree with, or would change, and gives a reason. At least one sentence carries an opinion word such as I think or in my view.
writing.support: Write two lines first: I agree with , because , and I would change , because . Then turn each line into three sentences.
writing.extension: End with one sentence of advice of your own, using should or ought to.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which word?
activities.instructions:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: advice, advise, guidance, encourage, discourage, warn, reassure, tip.
1. What another person tells you they think you should do is ____ .
2. When you tell somebody what you think they should do, you ____ them.
3. To tell somebody that a thing may go wrong is to ____ them.
4. To say calm, true things to a worried person is to ____ them.
5. To say things that make somebody want to keep going is to ____ them.
6. To say things that make somebody want to stop is to ____ them.
7. One short, useful piece of help is a ____ .
8. Help of a general kind, given over time, is ____ .
activities.answers:
1. advice  2. advise  3. warn  4. reassure  5. encourage  6. discourage  7. tip  8. guidance
Items 1 and 2 are the pair people swap. Advice is the thing; advise is what you do.
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the cards for the ones you missed. Five or fewer: read all eight cards again, then do this once more.
activities.solo: Cover the word list with your hand for the first four items. Uncover it only if you are stuck, and mark which ones needed it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Should, ought to or needn't?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word for each gap. Use should, ought to or needn't.
1. You ____ write it down. It is a good idea.
2. You ____ fill in the long form. There is no need.
3. She ____ give herself twenty minutes. It would help her.
4. You ____ ring them. The notice says it online.
5. He ____ say it out loud. It is the best tip in the unit.
6. We ____ book a desk to read here. Desks 13 to 20 are free.
7. They ____ study when they are too tired. It is a bad idea, so use the negative.
8. ____ I report the broken chair in writing? Ask the question.
activities.answers:
1. should (or ought to)  2. needn't  3. ought to (or should)  4. needn't  5. should (or ought to)  6. needn't  7. shouldn't  8. Should
Item 7 is the only negative advice. Shouldn't means a bad idea; needn't would mean there is no need.
Six or more right: go on. Five or fewer: read card 1 again and do items 2, 4 and 6 once more.
activities.solo: Do items 1 to 4, check them, then do 5 to 8. Checking halfway stops one wrong idea running through all eight.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Put the self word in
activities.instructions:
Write the missing self word in each gap.
1. I taught ____ to cook.
2. She booked the desk ____ .
3. He was working by ____ all evening.
4. We found the answer ____ in the end.
5. They taught ____ from a book.
6. Help ____ to a mug of tea.
7. I reminded ____ to take the receipt.
8. She let ____ into the room.
activities.answers:
1. myself  2. herself  3. himself  4. ourselves  5. themselves  6. yourself  7. myself  8. herself
Items 2 and 8 use the same word for two different jobs. In 2 it means without help; in 8 she is the one it happens to.
Six or more right: go on. Five or fewer: write the six self words in a column beside I, you, he, she, we, they, and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each finished sentence out loud before you check. A wrong self word usually sounds wrong before it looks wrong.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Which small word?
activities.instructions:
Write the missing small word. Use for, of, on, with, in, by or at.
1. I am responsible ____ the keys.
2. She is capable ____ doing it alone.
3. He is keen ____ early starts.
4. Are you satisfied ____ the answer?
5. Please send your reply ____ writing.
6. The form must be filled in ____ hand.
7. ____ last, the parcel arrived.
8. He left the light on, ____ purpose.
activities.answers:
1. for  2. of  3. on  4. with  5. in  6. by  7. At  8. on
Items 1 to 4 are adjectives that bring their own small word. Items 5 to 8 are fixed phrases with no rule inside them.
The likeliest wrong answers are 1 as of and 6 as with. Responsible always takes for; by hand is fixed.
Six or more right: go on. Five or fewer: do cards 3 and 4 again, then redo this.
activities.solo: Sort the eight items into two lists before you answer: adjective pairs and fixed phrases. The two kinds are learnt in different ways.

activities.title: Practice 5 — How many out of the group?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word or verb form.
1. (Either / Both) day is fine. I do not mind which.
2. (Neither / Plenty) of my keys opens the door.
3. (Both of / Either of) the forms are on the desk.
4. (Several / Plenty) of the answers were wrong, so I did the page again.
5. There is (several / plenty) of time before the room shuts.
6. Neither of the quiet corners (is / are) free at six.
7. Both of the desks (was / were) booked by Monday.
8. Plenty of people (studies / study) here after work.
activities.answers:
1. Either  2. Neither  3. Both of  4. Several  5. plenty  6. is  7. were  8. study
Items 6 to 8 are all about the verb. Neither counts as one; both of and plenty of count as more than one.
Six or more right: go on. Five or fewer: read the verb lines on card 5 and do 6, 7 and 8 again.
activities.solo: For 6 to 8, cover the words after of and read the sentence again. Neither of my keys becomes neither, which takes is.

activities.title: Practice 6 — The advice and the reason
activities.instructions:
Read Reading 2 again. It gives advice and then a reason for it.
Match each piece of advice, 1 to 4, with its reason, a to d.
1. Do less, and do it more often.
2. Study for a short time rather than a long one.
3. Pick a time that already exists in your day.
4. Count the days you studied, not the hours.
a. Because a short session makes you choose the one thing you need, and say it out loud.
b. Because a long evening is hard to repeat, and repeating is the part that works.
c. Because you can see the result, and people who count nothing are disappointed later.
d. Because a habit built into something you already do costs very little effort.
Then write one sentence saying whether you agree with the writer, and why.
activities.answers:
1. b  2. a  3. d  4. c
1 and 2 are close, so read them carefully. 1 is about how often; 2 is about what a short session makes you do.
There is no right answer to the last sentence. Check only that yours has an opinion and a reason joined by because.
Four of four: go on. Two or three: find the paragraph each reason comes from and read it once more.
activities.solo: Write the numbers 1 to 4 on paper and put the letters beside them before you look at the key. Guessing and then checking teaches more than reading the key first.

quizzes.q: Which sentence gives advice rather than an order?
options: You should send it in writing.
You must send it in writing.
You cannot send it in writing.
quizzes.a: You should send it in writing.
quizzes.why: Should says it is a good idea, and the person may still decide. Must makes it necessary, the bare verb makes it an order, and cannot says it is not allowed. Must is the tempting one, because advice often feels strong.

quizzes.q: Which sentence says that a job is not necessary?
quizzes.why: Needn't means there is no need, so ringing is allowed and simply not required. Mustn't forbids it, shouldn't calls it a bad idea, and have to makes it necessary. Mustn't is the usual wrong choice, because both words look negative.

options: You should to write it down.
You ought to write it down.
quizzes.a: You ought to write it down.
quizzes.why: Ought keeps its to and should never takes one, so the first drops a needed to and the second adds one that does not belong. The last changes the verb, which stays plain after every one of these words.

options: I filled the form in me.
I filled the form in my self.
I filled the form in himself.
I filled the form in myself.
quizzes.a: I filled the form in myself.
quizzes.why: The doer is I, so the self word is myself, written as one word. Me is the plain object form, my self splits a single word in two, and himself names somebody else. My self is the tempting one because it looks like my bag.

quizzes.q: She taught ____ to drive. Which word fits?
quizzes.why: The woman who taught and the woman who learnt are the same person, so the word ends in self. Her would mean a second woman, herselves is not a word, and hers means the one belonging to her.

options: I am responsible of the keys.
I am responsible for the keys.
I am responsible on the keys.
quizzes.a: I am responsible for the keys.
quizzes.why: Responsible always brings for with it. Of is the commonest wrong choice because it is the everyday joiner between two nouns, the third drops the small word altogether, and on belongs to keen.

options: She is capable to do it alone.
She is capable of do it alone.
She is capable of doing it alone.
She is capable for doing it alone.
quizzes.a: She is capable of doing it alone.
quizzes.why: Capable takes of, and a verb after of ends in ing. The first uses the pattern that belongs to able to. The second keeps of but leaves the verb plain. The last swaps in the small word that belongs to responsible.

options: I am keen of early starts.
I am keen to early starts.
I am keen on early starts.
quizzes.a: I am keen on early starts.
quizzes.why: Keen brings on with it, in the same way that good brings at and interested brings in. Of and to are borrowed from other adjectives, and the third leaves the pair unfinished.

In writing is a fixed phrase and takes in. On and by are the small words people reach for from by hand and on purpose, and in write uses the wrong form of the word. Nothing inside the phrase can be worked out; it is learnt whole.

quizzes.q: Which phrase means after a long wait?
quizzes.why: At last marks the end of a long wait. At first points at the beginning instead, on purpose gives a reason, and by hand names the way a thing was done. At first is the tempting one, because both phrases start with at.

quizzes.q: I tried both keys and the door stayed shut. ____ of my keys opens it.
quizzes.why: Not one and not the other is neither, and the verb stays short: opens. Both would say the opposite, several needs more than two things, and either would mean one of them does work.

options: Either of the two days are fine.
Several of the answers were wrong.
quizzes.a: Several of the answers were wrong.
quizzes.why: Several of counts more than two things, so were is right. Either and neither each count as one, so the first two put a plural verb where a short one belongs. The third drops the the that of needs in front of a noun.

teacherNotes.note: The extra to after should is the error that lasts longest, because the learner has met so many verbs that take one. Explaining the rule again rarely helps; they already agree with it. What helps is a two-word drill: say should go, ought to go, should ring, ought to ring, ten pairs in a row, out loud. The ear learns the gap faster than the eye does. Practice 2 and Speaking 1 are built for that.

Mustn't and needn't look like the same negative and are opposites. Mustn't forbids; needn't removes a requirement and leaves the choice open. The clearest way in is a pair of real notices: you mustn't repair anything yourself, and you needn't book a desk to read here. Both are in the unit's notice, one line apart, so the learner can see the difference on a page rather than in a rule.

Neither of my keys opens it is the sentence that trips people up, because keys sits right in front of the verb. Cover everything after of and read what is left: neither opens it. That test works for either of, both of, several of and plenty of too, and it is quicker than remembering which word is singular.

Every piece of advice in this unit is about learning English or about an ordinary task in a building: booking a desk, reporting a broken chair, choosing a time to study. That is deliberate. If a learner brings a question about health, money or papers to a study session, the honest answer is that this unit cannot help with it and a person who knows that subject should be asked. The language patterns transfer; the advice does not.

The tutor works best here as a rehearsal partner rather than a judge. Useful prompts: ask it for six situations and answer each with one should sentence and one needn't sentence; ask it to stop before the last word of a sentence so the learner supplies the self word; ask it to name the small word after responsible, capable and keen every time the learner gets one wrong. Do not let it mark the writing tasks; the criteria under each task are countable and the learner can check them alone.

selfAssessment.statement: I can tell someone what they should do and what they needn't do.
I can say that I did something myself.
I can write what I am responsible for and what I am keen on.
I can use set phrases like in writing and by hand with the right small word.
I can choose between either, neither, both of and plenty of, and use the right verb.
I can listen to advice and say what reason was given for it.
I can find the writer's opinion in a short text and work out a new word from the sentence around it.
I can say what I think of advice someone gives me, and why.

assignment.title: Advice for the person who comes after you
assignment.instructions:
Make one recording and write one short page. You may invent every detail.
Part 1. The recording, about one minute.
Give advice to somebody who starts learning English next month.
Say three things they should or ought to do. Keep the verb plain after each one.
Say two things they needn't do at all.
Say one thing you did yourself, using a self word.
Say what they will be responsible for, and one thing they are already capable of.
End with the tip you are most keen on, and give one reason for it.
Play the recording back and count the eight things in that list.
If one is missing, record the whole minute again. Do not add it in your head.
Part 2. The written page.
Write two paragraphs of four to five sentences.
Paragraph one: your advice, with should, ought to and needn't.
Paragraph two: what you think of the advice in Reading 2, and why.
Under the two paragraphs, write three short lines about yourself.
One with responsible for, one with capable of, one with keen on.
Check three things before you finish.
No to after should or needn't, and the verb plain after both.
Every self word matches its person: I with myself, she with herself, they with themselves.
Either and neither take the short verb; both of, several of and plenty of take the long one.
Then write one line that starts: This shows I can …
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and a written page
